papers.title: Evidence-Gated Scholarly RAG
references: Lewis et al. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. 2020. doi:10.5555/3495724.3496517
chunks:
Abstract
This study evaluates evidence-gated scholarly retrieval augmented generation.

Methodology
We sampled 200 claims from 50 computer-science papers and used three blinded annotators.

Experiments
Table 1: Accuracy by retrieval method
F1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) (1)

Results
We find the cross-encoder reranker improves citation accuracy from 81 percent to 93 percent.

Results
The evidence gate reduces unsupported claims by 35 percent.

Limitations
However, the study is limited to English computer-science papers and one annotation protocol.

References
[1] Lewis et al. Retrieval-Augmented Generation. 2020. doi:10.5555/3495724.3496517

papers.title: Replication of Scholarly Reranking
references: Smith et al. Citation Verification. 2025. doi:10.1234/verify
chunks:
Abstract
This replication evaluates cross-encoder evidence reranking.

Methodology
We evaluated 180 claims from 45 biomedical papers with two independent reviewers.

Experiments
Table 2: Replication accuracy
error_rate = unsupported / total (2)

Results
We find the cross-encoder reranker does not improve citation accuracy and lowers it from 82 percent to 78 percent.

Results
Open-access resolution successfully retrieves 96 percent of available full-text papers.

Limitations
However, the replication is limited to biomedical abstracts and excludes paywalled full text.

References
[1] Smith et al. Citation Verification. 2025. doi:10.1234/verify

The reported F1 is the harmonic combination of precision and recall.
The replication evaluated 180 claims from 45 biomedical papers with two reviewers.
The reranker lowers citation accuracy from 82 percent to 78 percent.
Open-access resolution retrieves 96 percent of available full-text papers.
The replication is limited to biomedical abstracts and excludes paywalled full text.
